title: Why God Refused to Answer
overview: When leaders of the exiles come to ask God for guidance, God refuses and instead retells Israel's long history of turning to other gods, then promises both judgment and a future restoration.

parts.label: Elders turned away (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: About seven years into the exile in Babylon, around 591 BC, some leaders came to Ezekiel to hear from God. God refuses to be consulted by people still clinging to idols and tells Ezekiel to confront them with their ancestors' record instead.

parts.label: Rebellion in Egypt and wilderness (vv. 5-17)
parts.note: God chose Israel as slaves in Egypt and swore with a raised hand, an ancient oath gesture, to give them a good land, yet they kept Egypt's gods and ignored God's laws and Sabbaths, which were meant as a sign of their bond. God spared them 'for the sake of my name,' meaning to protect God's reputation among watching nations, though that generation was barred from the land.

parts.label: The next generation repeats it (vv. 18-26)
parts.note: Their children were told not to copy their parents but did the same, so God swore they would one day be scattered among the nations. Verses 25 and 26 are hard and debated: many read them as God handing the people over to their own deadly practices, even sacrificing firstborn children, while others see a twisted misuse of the command to dedicate firstborns to God.

parts.label: Hilltop shrines and the present (vv. 27-32)
parts.note: In the land they worshiped at hilltop shrines, called 'high places,' and Ezekiel says his own generation still burns children as offerings. Some exiles want to blend in and worship idols of wood and stone like other nations, and God says flatly this will not happen.

parts.label: A new exodus with judgment (vv. 33-44)
parts.note: God promises to gather the scattered people as in the first exodus, checking them like a shepherd counting sheep under his staff and removing the rebels. Those who remain will worship on God's holy mountain, look back on their past with shame, and be treated according to God's own character rather than what they deserved.

parts.label: Fire in the southern forest (vv. 45-49)
parts.note: Ezekiel pictures an unstoppable fire burning every tree, green and dry, in the south, which the next chapter shows means Judah and Jerusalem. People dismiss him as a mere teller of riddles, and in Hebrew Bibles these verses begin chapter 21.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promised regathering in verses 33 to 44 was fulfilled in the return from Babylon, still awaits a future regathering of the Jewish people, or is fulfilled spiritually in the church.
think: When a family, community or nation keeps repeating the same failures across generations, what do you think it would actually take to break the pattern?
